keyVerseText: Now the birth of Jesus Christ was on this wise: When as his mother Mary was espoused to Joseph, before they came together, she was found with child of the Holy Ghost.
rootMeaning: The Greek verb ἔχω (échō) is a primary verb whose core meaning centers on the concept of holding or possessing. This root sense encompasses a wide range of applications, from physically holding something in one's hand to figurative possession or condition. Unlike the simple English gloss 'have,' the original sense implies a continuous or relational state, indicating not just possession but also the ongoing nature of holding or maintaining something.
usageInScripture: With 710 occurrences in the New Testament, ἔχω is frequently translated as 'have,' 'hath,' or 'having,' reflecting its broad semantic range. Its usage spans from literal physical holding to figurative expressions of possession, ability, or condition, as seen in the variety of top translations such as 'hath' (80 times) and 'have' (71 times). This consistency in translation highlights its fundamental role in expressing possession and relational continuity in Scripture.
theologicalSignificance: Understanding ἔχω enriches our grasp of biblical texts by revealing how possession and relationship are conveyed in the original language. It underscores the reality that faith involves not only receiving but continuously holding onto spiritual truths and blessings. In Christ-centered theology, this verb reminds believers that they 'have' not just a momentary gift but an enduring possession in Christ, who holds all things together. The verb’s range, including ability and condition, also points to the believer’s empowered state through the Holy Spirit, emphasizing both possession and active participation in God’s kingdom.
keyVerseReflection: In Matthew 1:18, the phrase 'she was found with child of the Holy Ghost' implicitly involves the concept of ἔχω in the sense of possessing or holding a condition—in this case, Mary bearing the Holy Spirit's child. The use of ἔχω here highlights the reality and continuity of the miraculous conception, emphasizing that Mary 'had' or 'held' this divine presence within her before coming together with Joseph. This enriches the understanding of the incarnation as an ongoing, tangible possession of the Spirit’s work in her.
